prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Lines of Action on an 8x8 board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(board) -> str: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move when `policy` is called. - `board` is an 8x8 grid of ints with the following encoding: - `0` represents an empty cell. - `1` represents your piece (current player). - `-1` represents the opponent's piece. - Rows are indexed from `0` (top) to `7` (bottom). - Columns are indexed from `0` (left) to `7` (right). - Rules summary (Lines of Action): - Players alternate moves. - A piece moves horizontally, vertically, or diagonally. - A piece must move exactly as many squares as there are pieces (both players) in the line (row, column, or diagonal) of movement. - A piece may jump over friendly pieces but may not jump over enemy pieces. - A piece may land on and capture an enemy piece (removing it from the board). - Objective: connect all of your pieces into a single contiguous group, where connectivity is counted in 8 directions (horizontal/vertical/diagonal). # Action / Return Format - Return a single move string formatted exactly as: `"from_row,from_col:to_row,to_col"`. - All coordinates are 0-indexed with `row,col` in `0..7`. - The move must be legal according to the Lines of Action rules. - Example (syntax only): `"0,1:2,3"` moves the piece from `(0,1)` to `(2,3)`. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm planning a Lines of Action policy using alpha-beta search with an evaluation based on connectivity and centralization, working within a 1-second time budget, and making sure it always returns a legal move even in edge cases like having no legal moves or only one piece left. I'm now thinking through move generation, iterating over each piece and its possible directions.

I'll use a flat 64-element array for the board to keep things fast, scanning for pieces each time rather than maintaining separate sets. For move generation, I'm checking each of the four axes from a piece's position, counting pieces in both directions along that line to determine the move distance, then validating the destination square.

For evaluation, I'm thinking through whether to do it from a fixed perspective versus using negamax with color flipping, and I'll also need connectivity checking via flood fill to count how many separate groups each player's pieces form.

Now I'm defining the score for each player using two components: a heavy penalty for having pieces split across multiple disconnected groups, and a piece-square table that rewards central squares over edge and corner positions.

I'm also considering adding a concentration penalty based on distance from the center of mass, and thinking about whether to weight material or mobility -- probably keeping those minimal since captures can help or hurt connectivity depending on which side loses pieces. For win detection, I need to check connectivity after each move, accounting for the rule that a player wins if their stones are fully connected, even if the move was a capture that incidentally connects the opponent too.

Now I'm working out the scoring weights, balancing the penalty for having multiple disconnected components against the positional table values, trying to find a reasonable scale so the evaluation function properly favors connecting pieces over just improving position.

For time management, I'm planning iterative deepening with an 0.85-second budget, falling back to the last completed depth if a deeper search times out, and estimating how deep alpha-beta with decent move ordering can realistically reach given the branching factor and per-node cost.

For move ordering, I'll prioritize the previous iteration's best move at the root, then captures, then a quick positional score difference between destination and origin squares, plus checking for immediate winning moves at the root first. I'll skip Zobrist transposition tables for now to keep things simple.

Writing move generation code...

Finishing the connectivity check with BFS, then noting a bytearray might beat a set for speed. I'm starting to sketch evaluation logic per side, considering the edge case where a side has zero pieces.

The concentration measure isn't perfectly comparable across different piece counts, but that's an acceptable simplification. I'm now sketching the negamax search function with time-check logic and move generation, returning the evaluation when no moves are available.

The move loop tries each move, checks for immediate wins via connectivity, falls back to evaluation at shallow depth, or recurses otherwise, then undoes the move. I'm noting that opponent connectivity only needs rechecking after a capture, since that's the only way their piece structure changes.

For scoring, I'll bias faster wins by adding remaining depth to the win value. I'll add a periodic time check every 256 nodes that throws once the budget runs out, use iterative deepening at the root with immediate return on a winning move, and wrap everything in a try/except with a safe fallback to the first legal move. I also need to handle board input that might be numpy arrays, and I'm setting up move ordering using capture bonuses plus piece-square table deltas.

I'm also weighing in a connectivity term for move ordering, counting adjacent friendly pieces near the destination and origin squares, and defining the overall evaluation as the difference between each side's positional score. I'm double-checking the edge case where a side has zero pieces, since that situation shouldn't actually arise given the game rules.

For terminal states, I'll treat a connected side as a win and set the connectivity check to return false when a side has no pieces, so that case cleanly resolves to a loss. For search depth, I'm planning to start shallow and iteratively deepen up to around six plies within a time budget of roughly 0.8 seconds, keeping an eye on how expensive move generation will be in Python.

Estimating the cost per node: scanning move directions across pieces plus connectivity and evaluation checks adds up to a few hundred microseconds per node, and with roughly thirty candidate moves per position, a full depth-3 search tree could approach a second even with alpha-beta pruning trimming the branching factor.

I could speed up the connectivity check further but that risks complexity for marginal gain, so I'll skip a transposition table and incremental component tracking to keep things simple and bug-free. I'll set the time budget to around 0.8 seconds to leave some margin against unexpected overhead.

Now let me finalize the implementation.
